results.title: AWS Raised GPU Rental Prices Twice in 2026. Nebius Just Did It Again. — AIntOps
highlights:
AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block pricing for GPU instances roughly 15% in January 2026 and another 20% in July. Nebius raised its on-demand GPU prices again on October 1 — the second increase in three months, with some memory pricing up about 41%. Neither company frames these as one-time corrections. They read as a new baseline: the rental price of a GPU is no longer a number you can assume holds from one quarter to the next.

Published October 19, 2026 · 7 min read

## AWS: two hikes, one product line

AWS's EC2 Capacity Block pricing for ML instances moved twice this year. The first increase, reported to take effect around January 4-6, raised rates on the P5 family by roughly 15% — p5e.48xlarge went from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour, and p5en.48xlarge from $36.18 to $41.61. Asked about the change, an AWS spokesperson told Data Center Dynamics it reflects "the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter." The second increase landed July 1, roughly 20%, across the P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de families — one report lists the P6-B300 now billing at $14.04 per accelerator-hour. Both changes applied specifically to Capacity Block reservations, not general on-demand EC2 pricing.

## Nebius: the same pattern, a shorter interval

Nebius notified customers on September 17 that on-demand AI cloud prices would rise again starting October 1 — its second increase in roughly three months. The headline move: H100 GPU-hour pricing went from $3.85 to $4.50, about 17%, with some memory pricing up roughly 41%. The company's own framing points to tight capacity, the same pressure AWS cited.

...

This is our reading, not something either company states directly: a price increase on a GPU rental line reads like an infrastructure cost, not an AI cost, in most reporting structures — it shows up in a cloud bill, under compute, often in a different review than the one that tracks OpenAI or Anthropic API spend. If your AI workload runs partly on rented GPU capacity and partly on provider APIs, the two cost lines move independently and get reviewed by different people, on different schedules, even though both are the same underlying pressure: AI demand outpacing supply.

...

Neither AWS nor Nebius has signaled this is the last increase. Two rounds in a year, from two unrelated providers, each citing supply and demand rather than a one-off event, is a pattern worth budgeting for rather than treating as an anomaly to absorb once and move past.

results.title: Nebius raises GPU list prices up to 21% while H100 spot sits at $0.79 - CTOL Digital Solutions
highlights:
Posted prices for four Nebius GPU types rose 17 to 21 percent on 1 October. Its own spot board shows Blackwell chips near 60 percent of list and an H100 at the floor, so the squeeze sits in particular chips and regions.

Nebius told CNBC this week that AI computing prices are rising faster than it expected. On 1 October it lifted the posted price of four GPU types by 17 to 21 percent. Anyone renting GPUs has to decide whether that posted price is what they will pay.

The posted price mostly is not what buyers pay. It rose, but the price at which capacity actually clears is uneven, and Nebius now publishes it. Scarcity is specific to Blackwell chips and some regions, while older H100 capacity is sitting idle.

### What changed in the price list

The Nebius pricing documentation dates two changes. The first took effect on 1 October, when on demand prices per GPU hour rose for four chips. Reuters reported on 17 September that Nebius had announced it, its second price rise in three months.

- B300 went from $7.85 to $9.50, up 21.0 percent, the largest rise.
- B200 went from $7.15 to $8.50, up 18.9 percent.
- H200 went from $4.50 to $5.40, up 20.0 percent.
- H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50, up 16.9 percent, the smallest rise of the four.

The RTX PRO 6000 stayed at $1.80, so the rise did not reach every GPU.

The second change came on 8 October. The preemptible tier, which rents interruptible capacity at a discount, stopped using fixed prices. It moved to dynamic spot pricing that can change every 15 minutes.

One rule in the documentation matters most. The highest spot price is always one cent below the current on demand rate, so the new list price is a ceiling. The floor is $0.79 or $0.99 depending on the chip. The posted price rise matters to a spot buyer only when the market pushes against that ceiling.

...

On 21 October Nebius announced public live spot pricing, also shown on Shadeform, Silicon Data and GPU Finder. Nebius's spot board shows how far below the ceiling each chip sits. At 23:03 UTC on Wednesday, B300 cleared at $5.29 to $5.89 across three regions, 56 to 62 percent of list.

B200 cleared at $4.40 and $4.50, which is 52 and 53 percent of list. Across five Blackwell regions, then, spot cleared at 52 to 62 percent of list. That is 38 to 48 percent below the posted price, well above the floor, and still far under the ceiling.

H200 prices split sharply by region. In eu-north1 it cleared at $2.00, 37 percent of the $5.40 list. In eu-west1 it cleared at $5.09, 94 percent, so one chip showed a spread of 2.5 times between two regions.

H100 trades at the floor. It trades at $0.79 in eu-north1, its only region, and has done since 9 October at 17:01 UTC. Across the 12 markets on the board, the median spot price is about 57 percent of list.

...

Crusoe's on demand H200 and H100 sit below Nebius's list. Its pricing page lists on demand H200 at $4.29 an hour, 21 percent under Nebius's posted price. H100 is $3.90, and B300 is $9.90 against $9.50 at Nebius.

results.title: GPU prices are rising for a reason that has nothing to do with GPUs. | Compute Stacker
results.author: Compute Stacker
highlights:
What's reported but not confirmed: NVIDIA raising AI server system prices by around 15 to 17%. That comes from press reporting, not from NVIDIA.

The visible end of this is rate cards. Nebius raised H100 on-demand 16.9% and B300 21% on October 1, its second increase in three months. AWS raised reserved Capacity Block rates on October 7.

What it means for planning:

- Treat current list prices as a snapshot, not a trend line. Two major providers repriced within a week this month.
- If you're negotiating a commitment, the component cost environment is an argument both ways. Ask what happens if memory prices fall.
- Spot and preemptible tiers absorb this differently from committed contracts. Nebius's October 1 increase didn't touch committed contracts.
- Check your provider's rate card before you budget, not after.

results.title: Is GPU compute tight? The answer is in contract length | SecondSource
highlights:
CoreWeave, a cloud company that specializes in renting out GPUs, the chips AI runs on, says rental prices rose about 25% starting in July. Yet a public index that the website getdeploying compiles from the list prices on dozens of providers' websites read only a 5% rise over a year in mid-September. Both numbers can be right. Almost all of CoreWeave's revenue comes from customers on contracts, while the index collects only the hourly, stop-any-time prices listed on websites (pay-as-you-go), so the two numbers measure different prices. Where compute is visibly tight, with more would-be renters than machines, is contract length: customers who sign for only three to six months pay 2.5 to 4 times the price of a five-to-six-year contract. That is above the gap of about 2 times between renting by the hour and signing for three years in the public market (SecondSource's conversion), but the two multiples cover different terms, so the gap can only be called high. No multiple calculated the same way exists for earlier years, so how much tighter than in past years cannot be said. Long contracts also require 20% to 30% up front. In October, after another provider raised list prices, the index's one-year rise reached 18%. CoreWeave's third-quarter results will show how fast new prices lift the average price across all of CoreWeave's contracts.

...

## Six: In October, another company's listed prices moved

For the week of October 12, getdeploying's reading became 9% over four weeks and 18% over a year; SecondSource's recomputation from getdeploying's public weekly data matches. In the same period Nebius, another GPU rental company, raised listed prices from October 1 (Nebius pricing page). The H100 went from US$3.85 to US$4.50 an hour, and the increases across the H100 and three other NVIDIA GPU models, the H200, B200 and B300, ranged from 17% to 21%.

So the public index can see price increases; what the index sees are increases in listed prices. The index is calculated by GPU model, and in the week of October 12, 21 of 26 models rose; getdeploying hasn't broken out which providers changed prices or how much each contributed.

...

| Contract | Price, autumn 2026 | Term, and whether the customer can leave early | Source of the figure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay-as-you-go listed | H100 median US$3.51 an hour (40 providers); specialist GPU clouds US$4.50; big clouds such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google US$7.89; Silicon Data's specialist-cloud H100 rental index US$2.82 on October 17, +6.4% over seven days | Stop at any time | Third-party compilation of listed prices |
| One-year contract | H100 US$1.70 → US$2.35 an hour (October 2025 to March 2026) | One year | Silicon Data figures cited by SemiAnalysis |
| Three-to-six-month contract | CoreWeave about US$40 million per MW per year, about US$7.6 to US$8.4 per GPU per hour | Three to six months | Company-reported |
| Cancellable big order | Google pays SpaceX US$920 million a month to rent 110,000 GB200s, about US$11.6 per GPU per hour, about US$55 million to US$60 million per MW per year | Three years on paper, cancellable on 90 days' notice | Four outlets report the same figures; unit price estimated by SecondSource |
| Five-to-six-year contract | IREN–NVIDIA about US$11.3 million; IREN–Microsoft about US$9.7 million; Nebius–Microsoft at least US$11.6 million; OpenAI–Oracle about US$13.3 million; Nscale–Anthropic about US$16 million (six years); all per MW per year | Five to six years, 20% to 30% prepaid | Press releases, filings and reporting; calculated by SecondSource |
| CoreWeave company-wide average | About US$6.9 million to US$8.2 million per MW per year | All contracts | SecondSource's rough calculation |

...

Details of the public index. Each week getdeploying records every provider's pay-as-you-go listed price. getdeploying takes a median for each provider and then a median across providers, one vote per provider, leaving out reserved and spot prices. SecondSource recomputed October 12 against September 14 from getdeploying's public weekly data: the median change across the 26 models is 8.6%, and against October 13, 2025 it is 18.2%. Nebius's new prices from October 1 were reported by the press by September 17 (Investing.com): the H100 from US$3.85 to US$4.50, the H200 from US$4.50 to US$5.40, the B200 from US$7.15 to US$8.50 and the B300 from US$7.85 to US$9.50. Several outlets called it the second increase in three months. All five data-center models in the index rose between September 14 and October 12: the H100 from US$3.34 to US$3.51, the H200 from US$4.44 to US$4.86, the B200 from US$6.52 to US$7.99, the B300 from US$7.87 to US$8.99 and the A100 from US$1.75 to US$1.82. The rise is uneven across generations: the H100 is up 5% over four weeks, the B200 up 23%. Compute Desk, another index provider, builds its index from completed transactions. Compute Desk says the B300 pay-as-you-go price rose 17 days in a row to a record on October 15, at about US$7 to US$10 an hour, about 64% above November 2025. That account comes from a single secondhand source. The September 18 call also said that a near-double-digit quarterly rise in the public index in the fourth quarter would mean the two measures had converged. A 9% rise over four weeks is already close, but what rose is the listed price itself.

The big-cloud layer. On getdeploying's listed medians, the H100 costs US$7.89 at big clouds and US$4.50 at specialist GPU clouds, 75% higher. The H200 is 101% higher and the B200 68% higher. Silicon Data's head of research said in late September that big clouds often charge two to three times or more what specialist GPU clouds charge, because other services are bundled in. For that reason Silicon Data lists big clouds separately and keeps them out of its index. Silicon Data's late-July report said the gap narrowed from about 250% in early 2025 to about 120% in the third quarter. Tightness at this layer shows up as customers who can't get capacity, not in list prices. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said in late July that Amazon had raised 2026 capital spending to about US$220 billion and still could not meet this year's demand, and that next year would be the same (Fortune).

results.title: Nebius spot GPUs: what you save when the machine can stop — Para Tu Rato
results.author: Para Tu Rato
highlights:
Nebius on-demand rates before and from October 1, 2026, in dollars per GPU-hour. This does not show spot prices. Checked October 18. Original Para Tu Rato chart.

# Nebius spot GPUs: what you save when the machine can stop

October’s changes raise on-demand rates and make spot pricing variable. We examine rates, interruptions and a ten-useful-hour calculation to compare the cost of completing a task.

Para Tu Rato 19.10.2026 6 min read

...

Renting a GPU for an experiment can feel liberating: a task that will not fit on your computer becomes possible. But the hourly rate tells only part of the story. If the machine stops before the process saves results, the next session begins by recovering lost ground. Before choosing interruptible capacity, compare the cost of reaching the same completed result.

## Two October changes

On-demand rates rose on October 1. On October 8, those GPUs and RTX PRO 6000 moved from fixed preemptible discounts to variable spot prices. [1]

## On-demand rates

USD/GPU-hour, excluding tax. Calculated changes. Storage is charged separately, including while the machine is stopped. [1]

- H100 ↗ — $3.85 → $4.50 · +16.9 %
- H200 ↗ — $4.50 → $5.40 · +20 %
- B200 ↗ — $7.15 → $8.50 · +18.9 %
- B300 ↗ — $7.85 → $9.50 · +21 %

## “From $0.79” does not reserve an H100

The public page lists H100 and H200 from $0.79 per GPU-hour, and B200 and B300 from $0.99. These are published floors, not booked session prices. Nebius also lists storage charges. Separate GPU rental from resources that keep accumulating costs while you wait for another available window. [2]

## A ceiling limits price, not continuity

Spot prices can change every fifteen minutes, including during a run. Set a maximum and you pay the current spot price, not that maximum; the machine stops if the price exceeds it. Alternatively, follow spot without your own ceiling. Neither guarantees capacity: Nebius may reclaim it for other work. A spending boundary and the ability to finish are separate conditions. [3]

results.title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP Cloud GPU Pricing [2026]
results.author: Sana Rahman
highlights:
Cloud GPU pricing used to be a simple spreadsheet exercise: look up the hourly rate for an H100 instance, multiply by the hours you need, pick the cheapest provider. In October 2026 that spreadsheet broke. AWS raised its Blackwell B200 Capacity Block rate by roughly 15% on October 7, Microsoft Azure is one of the only major clouds still publishing a flat per-GPU hourly rate for H100 capacity, and Google Cloud has yet to post an official list price for H100, H200 or B200 instances at all. Comparing AWS vs Azure vs GCP cloud GPU pricing now means comparing three different billing philosophies, not just three price tags.

...

The three major hyperscalers no longer sell GPU capacity the same way. AWS leans heavily on EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, a reservation product with dynamic pricing that changes with supply and demand rather than a fixed rate card. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks documentation confirms Capacity Blocks can reserve up to 64 instances, or as many as 512 H100 GPUs, with reservations bookable up to eight weeks in advance. That flexibility is useful for training runs with a known start date, but it also means there is no single “AWS H100 price” the way there used to be with plain on-demand EC2.

Microsoft Azure, by contrast, still publishes retail, pay-as-you-go rates for specific H100 virtual machine sizes. That transparency makes Azure the easiest provider to quote cleanly in a comparison article, which is exactly why most of the concrete numbers in this piece come from Azure’s own SKUs. Google Cloud sits at the opposite end: its A3 (H100), A3 Ultra (H200) and A4 (B200) instance families are confirmed to exist and to use those specific Nvidia GPUs, but no official Google Cloud page in the current research set states a public hourly price for any of them. Google increasingly routes customers toward Flex-start scheduling and committed-use contracts instead of a posted rate.

...

AWS maps its Nvidia GPU families onto a small set of EC2 instance types. According to AWS’s own documentation, the ml.p5.48xlarge family is built around H100 GPUs, while ml.p5e.48xlarge and ml.p5en.48xlarge carry H200 GPUs. The newer P6-B200 family moves to Blackwell-generation B200 GPUs, AWS also lists P6-B300 instances built around B300 GPUs as a newer, higher-tier option, and a P6e-GB200 UltraServer tier built around Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 rack-scale system for the largest training clusters. Each of these families is purchasable On-Demand, through Spot Instances, or through Savings Plans, and all of them are also eligible for Capacity Block reservations.

...

What AWS has not done, at least not in any officially confirmed source available as of October 23, 2026, is publish a flat on-demand hourly price for P5, P5e, P5en or P6-B200. Capacity Block pricing is explicitly dynamic, and AWS’s public materials direct buyers to request a quote or check the Capacity Blocks console rather than read a rate card.

...

Azure’s current GPU VM lineup for AI training includes NC40ads H100 v5, ND96isr H100 v5 and ND96isr H200 v5. Two of those SKUs give us the cleanest published numbers in this entire comparison. The NC40ads H100 v5 size, a single-H100 configuration, carried a reported East US pay-as-you-go Linux rate of $6.98 per hour as of October 19, 2026. The larger ND96isr H100 v5 size, which packs eight H100 GPUs, was reported at $98.32 per VM-hour in East US on the same date, which works out to $12.29 per GPU-hour.

Azure also lists an ND96isr H200 v5 size with eight H200 GPUs carrying 141 GB of memory each, making it the newest Hopper-class GPU family Azure has confirmed. Microsoft has not published an officially confirmed Azure B200 virtual machine family or hourly price as of October 23, 2026. Separately, Microsoft Foundry’s managed-compute tier, still in preview, bills hourly per accelerator across A100, H100, H200 and MI300 GPU families, but Microsoft’s documentation says rates vary by accelerator family, region, deployment scope and commitment term, and directs customers to the Azure Pricing Calculator rather than a published table.

...

Google Cloud confirmed on October 2, 2026 that its A3 instance family is powered by Nvidia H100 Tensor Core GPUs, while A3 Ultra instances carry Nvidia H200 Tensor Core GPUs. The newer A4 family, confirmed October 21, 2026, uses Nvidia HGX B200 GPUs, with the a4-highgpu-8g configuration packing eight B200 GPUs per instance. None of these three families has a confirmed, officially published public hourly price in the current research set. Google’s materials mention multiple consumption models for these instances, including on-demand, Spot and committed-use pricing, but do not spell out the specific rates for A3, A3 Ultra or A4.

...

| GPU | AWS (published rate) | Azure (published rate) | Google Cloud (published rate) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, single GPU | No flat rate published; Capacity Blocks price dynamically | $6.98/hour, NC40ads H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H100, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | $98.32/hour ($12.29/GPU-hour), ND96isr H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H200, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | No flat on-demand VM rate confirmed in official sources | Not published |
| B200, per GPU-hour (Capacity Block) | $14.208/hour, effective Oct. 7, 2026, up from $12.355/hour (about a 15% increase) | Not offered / not confirmed | Not published; A4 uses Flex-start scheduling instead of a flat rate |

...

## The October 7 AWS B200 Price Hike, Explained

The single clearest pricing move any of the three providers made in the last three months was AWS’s. Effective October 7, 2026, AWS raised its P6-B200 Capacity Block price from $12.355 to $14.208 per accelerator-hour, an increase of approximately 15%, according to GPU-pricing trackers Axis Intelligence and Dev.to’s FastGPU column, which independently captured the same before-and-after figures. For an eight-GPU P6-B200 node, the current instance-hour rate is about $113.666, a noticeable jump in monthly spend for teams running sustained training jobs.

AWS frames Capacity Block pricing as dynamic by design, moving with supply and demand rather than sitting on a fixed card, so a mid-quarter increase is consistent with how the product is supposed to work. It is also a useful data point for the “which cloud is cheapest” question: it shows that even the provider with the most reservation flexibility, AWS, is not necessarily the cheapest or the most stable option for Blackwell-class capacity right now. Teams planning a long B200 training run in Q4 2026 should budget for the possibility of another adjustment before their reservation window closes, since trackers reported this was not the first GPU list-price increase AWS made in recent months.

Published rate cards tell a different story from marketplaces. Our price board — built from the on-demand prices cloud providers publish — put the on-demand H100 hour at $4.11 on 13 Nov 2026, against a marketplace median of $3.93 in the week of 9 Nov 2026.

Neither number is “the” price. List prices show what providers ask for capacity on demand; marketplace medians show where spare capacity clears; reserved and contract prices, usually lower again, sit in agreements that are rarely published in full. For anyone valuing a neocloud, lending against GPUs or underwriting a datacentre lease, the spread between the three says how tight capacity is.
